source.title: Some Open Problems in the Dynamics of Quadratic and Higher Degree Polynomial ODE Systems

accepted.question_text: Determine rigorously whether the three-dimensional autonomous quadratic system x' = y^2 - z^2, y' = x, z' = y is non-chaotic. The system appears numerically to have a single unstable periodic solution and is conjectured to be non-chaotic; equivalently, decide the behavior of the associated jerk equation z''' = (z')^2 - z^2.

evidence.quote: 3.1. First Open Problem Several years ago Zhang and Heidel [Heidel & Zhang, 1999] and [Zhang & Heidel, 1997] showed that (almost) all dissipative and conservative three dimensional autonomous quadratic systems of ordinary differential equations with at most four terms on the right hand sides of the equations are non-chaotic. The sole exception is the system ... x0 = y 2 - z 2 ... y0 = x ... z 0 = y ... which does however appear numerically to have a single unstable periodic solution and is therefore conjectured to also be non-chaotic. The above system is equivalent to the third order or “jerk” equation z 000 = z 02 - z 2 . ... Thus carefully determining the behavior of solutions of equation (3.1) becomes an interesting problem instead of just being a passing curiosity.

accepted.question_text: Give a universal definition of non-chaotic solutions for continuous autonomous dynamical systems x' = f(x) on R^N. The definition should cover non-chaotic behavior beyond the authors' criterion that excludes bounded chaos when N-2 components of every solution eventually either tend to a finite limit, are periodic or asymptotic to a periodic function, are unbounded, or exhibit one of several finite-time behaviors; in particular, it should still work for N > 3, where that criterion remains unverified and incomplete.

evidence.quote: 3.2. Second Open Problem ... Giving a universal definition of non-chaotic solutions is another way to define chaotic solutions. It is known that it is also very difficult. In [Heidel & Zhang, 2007] we gave a conjecture on the criterion recognizing non-chaotic behavior: Consider the autonomous system x0 = f (x), x ∈ RN , t ∈ [0, ∞) ... Criterion 3.1. An N dimensional system (3.22) with no cluster points in the set of isolated fixed points has no bounded chaos if for any of its solutions there are N - 2 components ...

When N = 3 this criterion has been widely accepted. For N > 3 it still needs verification. Even if this criterion is very useful, it misses countless types of non–chaotic solutions. This open problem is to give a universal definition of non–chaotic solutions.

accepted.question_text: For autonomous polynomial systems x_i' = P_i(x) of degree at most k in N variables, determine which systems can have chaotic solutions after quotienting by natural equivalences. In particular: for N = 3 and given k, after eliminating scalar rescalings of the variables and time and quotienting by the order-three permutation group, determine which systems are chaotic, how many chaotic systems exist, and among them how many are conservative or dissipative; for N > 3 and given k, answer the analogous counting and classification question after quotienting by coordinate rescalings and the full permutation group; more generally, answer the same question up to affine equivalence x = Ay + b and identify which types of chaotic attractors can occur, for example Lorenz-type or Rössler-type attractors.
accepted.context_brief: classification and counting of chaotic polynomial systems

evidence.quote: 1. For a given k and N = 3 after eliminating equivalent systems under the scalar transformations x1 = aX1 , x2 = bX2 , x3 = cX3 , t = δτ ... which systems in the form of (3.23) have chaotic solutions and how many systems are chaotic? Among those chaotic systems how many of them are conservative, and how many of them are dissipative?

2. For any given integer N > 3 and k after eliminating equivalent systems under the scalar transformations ... and nth-order permutation groups Pg ... which systems in the form of (3.23) have chaotic solutions and how many systems are chaotic? Among those chaotic systems how many of them are conservative, and how many of them are dissipative?

3. More generally for a given N ≥ 3 after eliminating equivalent systems under affine transformations x0 = Ay + b, t = δτ ... which systems in the form of (3.23) have chaotic solutions and how many systems are chaotic? Among those chaotic systems how many of them are conservative, and how many of them are dissipative? 4. A related open problem is what types of chaotic attractors can the systems (3.23) have? Two examples of “types” of attractors are Lorenz attractor and Rössler attractor.

accepted.question_text: Let x' = f(x) be a polynomial or C^n vector field on R^3. If a trajectory is asymptotic to a two-dimensional C^r invariant manifold (r ≥ 1), can that trajectory still be chaotic, and if so how topologically complicated must the manifold be in order to contain or attract such chaos? In particular, can a quadratic differential equation on a torus exhibit chaos, and can a trajectory on a torus be more complicated than a space-filling curve?

evidence.quote: 3.4. Fourth Open Problem Consider x0 = f (x), x ∈ R3 , where f (x) are polynomials or f ∈ C n (R3 ), where n is a nonnegative integer. If a solution of the system is asymptotic to a 2D C r , r ≥ 1 an integer, invariant manifold, can the solution be chaotic? If such chaotic solutions exists, topologically how complicated the 2D manifold has to be? What we mean by a manifold being complicated topologically is that for example a torus can be considered more complicated than a plane. In particular, can a quadratic differential equation system on a torus exhibit chaos? In general can a solution of a system on a torus be more complicated than a space filling curve?

accepted.question_text: For the quadratic systems x' = y^2 - z + A, y' = z, z' = x and x' = y, y' = -x + yz, z' = 1 - y^2, prove that the numerically observed intersections of certain trajectories with their indicated Poincaré sections have fractal dimension, and then determine whether the corresponding systems are chaotic. Concretely, show that for the first system at least one trajectory intersects the section x = 0 in a set with nontrivial thickness, and that for the second system at least one trajectory intersects the section z = 0 in a set with nontrivial thickness; then decide whether those observations imply genuine chaos.

evidence.quote: 3.5. Fifth Open Problem From Fig. 3.2, and Fig. 3.3 it appears that system (3.24) has at least one solution such that it intersects the Poincaré section x = 0 into a set with “thickness”. Similarly from Fig. 3.4, it appears that system (3.25) has at least one solution that intersects the Poincaré section z = 0 into a set also with “thickness”. This open problem is to show that these sets have fractal dimensions. A further question is to show that this system is chaotic.

accepted.question_text: Give rigorous existence proofs of chaotic solutions for each of the following four three-dimensional quadratic autonomous systems, which were found numerically to have Rössler-type attractors: (i) x' = y^2 - x + Az, y' = x, z' = y; (ii) x' = yz - x + Ay, y' = z, z' = x; (iii) x' = yz + Az, y' = x - y, z' = y; (iv) x' = y^2 + Az, y' = x - y, z' = y.
accepted.context_brief: rigorous chaos proofs for four quadratic systems

evidence.quote: ... the following four systems are later studied in our work [Zhang & Heidel, 2010] ... System (3.27) and system (3.28) share the same scalar equation u000 = uu0 - u00 - Au in y and z respectively. The attractors are all of Rössler type. The open problem is to prove rigorously the existence of chaotic solutions in these systems: ... x0 = y 2 - x + Az ... y0 = x ... z 0 = y ... x0 = yz - x + Ay ... y0 = z ... z 0 = x ... x0 = yz + Az ... y0 = x - y ... z 0 = y ... x0 = y 2 + Az ... y0 = x - y ... z 0 = y.

needs_review.question_text_raw: The remaining 20 systems which are listed here are proved to be non-chaotic when the parameter in each of the systems is in certain range. Extensive computer simulations indicate that there are no chaotic attractors in these systems. We conjecture that they are non-chaotic systems.
